name: Monlunabant
lead: Monlunabant (also INV-202 and MRI-1891) is an investigational once-daily oral tablet that blocks the cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1), a receptor involved in appetite and energy balance. In the looksmaxxing context its relevance is body composition: in trials, people taking it lost weight and trimmed waist circumference, which is the route by which a leaner, more defined face and body is usually reached. It is not approved for any use and is available only inside clinical studies.[1][3][9]

The compound was discovered by researchers at the US National Institutes of Health, including Georges Kunos, Resat Cinar and Malliga Iyer, and developed by Inversago Pharma before becoming associated with Novo Nordisk.[1] It belongs to a drug class whose first member, rimonabant, was approved in Europe in 2006 and withdrawn in 2008-2009 over psychiatric adverse events. Monlunabant was designed to act mainly outside the brain to reduce that risk.[1][2]

A 16-week Phase 2a trial in adults with obesity and metabolic syndrome reported placebo-adjusted weight loss of roughly 6 to 8 kg across three doses, alongside dose-related gastrointestinal and psychiatric adverse events and a high rate of withdrawals at the highest dose.[3] Suicidal ideation was not reported in secondary summaries.[1]

paras: Monlunabant has no approved cosmetic use. Its appearance relevance follows from its intended purpose, reducing body weight and waist circumference in people with obesity. Trial participants had obesity and metabolic syndrome, and the studies measured body weight, waist circumference and metabolic markers rather than facial or aesthetic outcomes.[3][9]

The drug has been tested for obesity with metabolic syndrome and for diabetic kidney disease, where the aim was to lower urinary albumin.[3][6] The rationale for kidney disease comes partly from mouse work in which CB1 blockade added to the anti-fibrotic effect of SGLT2 inhibition.[10] A 2026 review describes peripherally restricted CB1 blockers as a developing area in obesity and metabolic disease.[8]

Monlunabant blocks the CB1 receptor, which is part of the endocannabinoid system that influences appetite, fat storage and glucose handling. It has been described as a beta-arrestin-2-biased CB1 antagonist, designed to act mainly in peripheral tissues such as the gut, liver and fat rather than the brain.[1][8]

A 2025 mouse study found that monlunabant reduced appetite and counteracted CB1-agonist-induced hypothermia, as rimonabant did, although it was consistently less potent than rimonabant. The authors concluded that it suppresses appetite through a central mechanism, suggesting that peripheral selectivity is incomplete.[4] Other mouse work found that it reduced alcohol-binge-induced intestinal permeability through gut CB1 receptors.[11]

Phase 1b: a 28-day randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of INV-202 (25 mg once daily) in 37 adults with features of metabolic syndrome found it well tolerated, with no serious or severe treatment-emergent events and mostly gastrointestinal side effects. Participants lost a mean 3.5 kg (3.3%) against a 0.6 kg gain with placebo, with significant reductions in waist circumference and BMI.[9]

Phase 2a in obesity: a 16-week randomised, double-blind, dose-ranging trial at 25 Canadian sites randomised 243 adults with obesity and metabolic syndrome to 10, 20 or 50 mg tablets or placebo. Versus placebo, mean weight change at week 16 was -6.4 kg at 10 mg, -6.9 kg at 20 mg and -8.0 kg at 50 mg. Adverse events, mainly mild to moderate gastrointestinal and psychiatric events, occurred in 69% on 10 mg, 78% on 20 mg, 92% on 50 mg and 69% on placebo. Withdrawals for adverse events were 13%, 27% and 42% at the three doses and none on placebo, with causes including nausea, anxiety, diarrhoea, irritability and sleep disorders. No deaths occurred. The authors concluded that weight loss was clinically meaningful at all doses, that higher doses added little, and that lower doses need further study.[3] Secondary summaries note more mild to moderate neuropsychiatric events than placebo, with no suicidal ideation reported.[1]
An open-label extension of the Phase 2a trial was published as a letter in Diabetes, Obesity & Metabolism in 2026, with authors from Novo Nordisk and the NIH.[5]

Diabetic kidney disease: a 16-week Phase 2 trial randomised 254 adults in the analysis set to 10 mg, 25 mg or placebo. Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratios fell in all groups (ratios to baseline of 0.58, 0.51 and 0.71), but the 25 mg group did not differ significantly from placebo (treatment ratio 0.72, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.14), so formal testing of 10 mg was not performed.[6]
A Phase 1 study of a single tablet in healthy-weight Japanese and Caucasian men (n=73) examined safety and blood concentrations.[7]

In the Phase 2a obesity trial, side effects were dose related, with nausea, diarrhoea, anxiety, irritability and sleep disturbance leading some participants to withdraw.[3] A 2026 review notes that the Phase 2 data showed dose-dependent psychiatric adverse events and that central effects were the reason centrally acting predecessors were discontinued.[8] Rimonabant carried depression and anxiety warnings, with suicidal ideation in about 1% of users.[2]

Rimonabant, discovered by Sanofi-Aventis, was approved by the European Commission in June 2006 as the first CB1 blocker. The FDA advisory committee voted against it in 2007, the European Medicines Agency recommended suspension in October 2008, sales were halted worldwide that November, and EU authorisation was withdrawn in January 2009.[2] The CRESCENDO trial reported psychiatric events such as anxiety, depression and insomnia in over 30% of patients.[2]

Peripherally restricted CB1 blockers followed as a way to keep metabolic benefits while avoiding central toxicity.[8] Monlunabant was reported by Novo Nordisk in 2024 to produce modest weight loss with neuropsychiatric effects, as cited by Wikipedia from STAT.[1] The Phase 2a trial ran from September 2023 to January 2024 and was published in 2025.[3]

No community material on monlunabant was found in looksmaxxing forums. Interest in it comes through the broader conversation about weight-loss drugs such as GLP-1 agonists, with CB1 blockade a separate mechanism still in trials.

card.summary: An experimental oral CB1 blocker for weight loss that showed modest results and some neuropsychiatric side effects in Phase 2.
card.note: Investigational; same drug class as rimonabant, withdrawn over psychiatric effects.

quick.overview:
Monlunabant is an experimental pill that blocks the CB1 receptor to reduce appetite and improve metabolism. It was designed to work mostly outside the brain.

A 16-week Phase 2a trial reported modest weight loss, and it is not approved anywhere.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an inverse agonist at CB1, a receptor tied to appetite and energy balance. A 2025 study suggests part of its appetite effect is central.
quick.risks: The Phase 2a trial reported higher rates of mild to moderate anxiety and sleep disturbance than placebo; suicidal ideation was not reported. The earlier drug in this class, rimonabant, was withdrawn over psychiatric effects.

angle.text: Monlunabant is being studied as a weight-loss drug. In the Phase 2a trial, participants lost several kilograms more than placebo, and a Phase 1b study also recorded smaller waist circumference.[3][9] Any appearance effect would come through reduced body fat, and the drug is only accessible through trials.
